title: Two Yamahas? The Spin-off's Revenue Is Over 5x
description:
On July 10, 1955, the little motorbike that won the Mount Fuji hill climb had gone on sale less than five months earlier, sold by a company that made pianos. The motorbike company that entered it had been founded just nine days before.

We start with a broken organ in Hamamatsu in 1887: the first organ, judged unusable; the wooden propellers made from 1921; the machine tools that survived the bombing; and a top-secret order in 1953. Then today's ledger: the shareholdings have flipped, the motorbike company's revenue is over five times the piano company's, and KHS turns out to be the old partner of both Yamahas in Taiwan.

The legend of carrying the organ over Hakone on a shoulder pole is marked as "it's said"; claims with only one source say who made them.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are cartoon characters, not likenesses. People who died less than 70 years ago are not drawn, only hands and objects. No company logos appear on screen.

Information as of 2026-10-31

chapters.open-you: A piano company's motorbike on Mount Fuji's start line
chapters.motor-found: Nine days old, racing up Mount Fuji
chapters.fork-carry: Splitting off, with the tuning fork and the craft

t001.text: In Taiwan you surely know two Yamahas: one at bike shops, one at music class.

t002.text: Of the new motorbikes registered in Taiwan in 2025, over 125,000 were Yamahas.

t003.text: July 10th, 1955. A hill climb race up Mount Fuji.

t004.text: The last two winners were both Honda.

t005.text: On the start line sits a small, new motorbike.

t006.text: Strangely, it had gone on sale under five months earlier,

t007.text: and the company selling it made pianos.

t008.text: A war would leave this piano company something it never expected.

t009.text: And today, the piano Yamaha and the motorbike Yamaha stand in very different places.

t010.text: This file turns over 130 years of records, page by page.

t011.text: Are the piano Yamaha and the Yamaha you ride really one company?

t012.text: 68 years before that bike, a Hamamatsu primary school's organ broke.

t013.text: The school called a man who fixed medical equipment, Torakusu Yamaha.

t014.text: He fixed the organ, and did one more thing on the side: he drew its whole insides.

t015.text: Two months later, using those drawings, he built his own first organ.

t016.text: Here's the problem: who would say his organ actually worked?

t017.text: It's said he carried it on a shoulder pole over Hakone's mountains to Tokyo.

t018.text: He went to what became Tokyo University of the Arts.

t019.text: The verdict was one line: looks fine, out of tune, unusable.

t020.text: All that way, for one word: unusable. What would you have done?

t021.text: Remember Tokyo University of the Arts. It shows up again over 60 years later.

t022.text: No going home. A month in Tokyo, learning music theory from scratch.

t023.text: I admired him here: rejected, he didn't go home angry. He sat down and learned.

t025.text: All earlier flaws removed; it could replace imports.

t026.text: Learning to tune, he held a tuning fork in his hand.

t027.text: Yamaha's own guess: the tuning fork logo grew out of these days.

t028.text: In 1897, he founded Nippon Gakki and became its first president.

t029.text: The next year, the tuning fork became the company emblem.

t030.text: Upright pianos began in 1900, and two years later, a grand piano too.

t031.text: Piano woodwork skills later caught the eye of a client you'd never guess.

t033.text: In 1921, the army asked Nippon Gakki for wooden aircraft propellers.

t035.text: Because wooden propellers are pressed, layer upon layer,

t037.text: An old Yamaha Motor director put it bluntly in a company magazine:

t038.text: For this precise woodwork, piano skills were the best fit.

t039.text: Think of it: wood that sings and wood that flies, shaped by the same hands.

t041.text: By that magazine's count, Japan made 4,033 propellers in 1939,

t042.text: and 2,567 of them came from this piano company, about 60 percent.

t043.text: I first thought I'd misread it.

t044.text: Stranger still, that old director recalls an outsider was brought in

t046.text: His name was Soichiro Honda. Yes, that Honda.

t048.text: A big quake in late 1944; the next May, an air raid hit the factory.

t049.text: An instrument and propeller factory: what would be left?

t050.text: In the May raid, the Tenryu factory's wooden propeller works burned down.

t051.text: One night in late July, naval guns fired from the sea hit the factory directly.

t052.text: As the boss, you'd think it's all gone?

t053.text: Yet one batch of machines was long gone from the factory.

t054.text: About 800 machine tools were evacuated to the hillside Sakura factory.

t056.text: All the instrument woodworking machines and gear.

t057.text: That old director himself used one word: ironic.

t058.text: Remember that unexpected thing from the start? These propeller machines.

t059.text: Their first products then: low dining tables and xylophones.

t060.text: From propellers to dining tables. Just feel that drop.

t062.text: So here's the question: what could these leftover machines do?

t063.text: On November 7th, 1953, President Genichi Kawakami gave a top-secret order:

t064.text: Prototype a bike engine; mass-produce in a year.

t065.text: The company magazine adds: use the Sakura machines before they decay.

t066.text: That old director later wrote: these machines are what sparked Yamaha Motor.

t068.text: Finite wood caps how far instruments can grow.

t069.text: Do you know how many bike makers Japan had then?

t071.text: By 1953, 42 were left. The biggest, Honda, made 3,200 a month.

t072.text: Squeezing in this late, what did a piano company have?

t073.text: The first cylinder used piano iron-frame casting,

t074.text: and got mocked as a teapot.

t075.text: In under a year of work, the bike was done.

t076.text: On February 11th, 1955, it shipped from Nippon Gakki's new Hamana factory.

t077.text: Here's the oddity from the start: the catalog's lower right says Nippon Gakki.

t079.text: Remember Tokyo University of the Arts?

t080.text: It was an associate professor on its art side, and his students.

t081.text: Nicknamed the Red Dragonfly, yet the two companies disagree on its color:

t082.text: The motorbike company says chestnut and cream; the piano company, crimson.

t083.text: One more problem: it was pricey.

t084.text: A 125 cc bike then averaged 110,000 to 120,000 yen. This one: 138,000.

t086.text: As the boss, would you keep making this bike?

t087.text: They didn't stop. They spun the whole motorbike division off.

t088.text: On July 1st, Yamaha Motor was founded.

t089.text: That's the Yamaha you ride today.

t090.text: Over 150 staff, two low wooden buildings,

t091.text: and a goal of 200 bikes a month, under a tenth of Honda's.

t092.text: Nine days later: the Fuji hill climb.

t093.text: How did that little bike on the line do?

t095.text: Of the top ten, seven were this bike.

t096.text: A company spun off from a piano maker held off Honda.

t097.text: For the autumn race, their engine tuning got even stranger.

t098.text: They used trombone resonance on the exhaust.

t099.text: Five horsepower became ten, two months later.

t100.text: To me, this is the cutest page in the file.

t101.text: Would the new bike company take the tuning fork too?

t103.text: Yamaha Motor says: even as a separate company,

t104.text: it would inherit Nippon Gakki's spirit. What do the three forks mean?

t105.text: Tech, production and sales working together,

t106.text: and music's melody, harmony and rhythm.

t107.text: At your next red light, check the bike ahead's badge.

t108.text: On the bike logo, the fork handles overlap the ring; on the piano one, they sit inside it.

t110.text: Craft. In 1965, Toyota signed with Yamaha Motor to co-develop a sports car.

t111.text: Its first retail car, two years later, had a wooden steering wheel, shift knob and dashboard,

t112.text: all from woodwork learned making instruments.

t113.text: A year after Toyota, the bike know-how reached Taiwan too. Who was the partner?

t114.text: KHS, which signed a technical aid deal in 1966.

t115.text: Surprise: KHS was also the piano side's old partner in Taiwan.

t116.text: A Taiwan University thesis says its Yamaha pianos were famous in the 50s and 60s,

t117.text: and in the 70s ran Yamaha music classes in Taiwan, sparking a kids' piano boom.

t118.text: Dragged to piano as a kid? You may be part of that wave.

t119.text: Around 1986, Yamaha Motor and KHS formed a joint venture, Yamaha Motor Taiwan.

t120.text: Doesn't this feel less like two companies, more like family?

t121.text: In 1987, its 100th year, Nippon Gakki renamed itself simply Yamaha.

t122.text: In 1996, the piano company also teamed with KHS, forming KHS Yamaha Musical Instruments.

t123.text: Such good friends, yet the ledger tells another story.

t124.text: In 2007, the piano company still held 22.7 percent of Yamaha Motor.

t125.text: That year it sold part, and the bike company stopped counting as its affiliate.

t126.text: In 2013, the piano company bought out the venture and renamed it Yamaha Music Taiwan.

t127.text: They also made a joint brand committee and shared rules,

t128.text: to manage the name they share.

t129.text: In 2015, they held a design show together, designing for each other:

t130.text: piano side designed vehicles; bike side, instruments.

t131.text: A lively show. But what about the piano side's shares?

t132.text: Later it sold several more blocks of Yamaha Motor stock.

t133.text: In January 2026, KHS also left the bike side,

t134.text: and Yamaha Motor Taiwan became wholly owned by Japan's Yamaha Motor.

t135.text: That August, the piano company sold 14 million more shares. What was left?

t137.text: In reverse, the bike company holds 3.2 percent of the piano company.

t138.text: Remember how the two Yamahas stand differently now? This is it.

t139.text: Stranger still, in late June Toyota held more Yamaha Motor stock than the piano company.

t140.text: If you hear piano Yamaha is the bike Yamaha's parent, the books disagree.

t141.text: Each is listed on its own. The piano company's profile is clear: they're run independently.

t142.text: So in business, who's bigger now?

t143.text: Back to the question: is the piano Yamaha the same company as the one you ride?

t144.text: Not the same. The spun-off bike firm's revenue is now over five times the piano one's.

t145.text: Anything at home stamped with those three forks? Comment below.

t146.text: This channel sticks to records you can check. Want to dig in with me? Subscribe.
